utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Martinovic and Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I think it's all right now. Cross-examined by Mr. Par: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will continue discussion from yesterday, starting with the events at the hospital where we left off yesterday. Let me remind you, we were dealing with the topic of Dzemo Skobalj, and I claimed he was not a member of Stela's unit. I would like to ask you how long you spent in the hospital, when you arrived and when you left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came there on the 16th of March and left on the 1st of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In that period, did you ever see Vinko Martinovic, Stela, in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any information that Stela was personally advised of incidents that took place at the hospital, such as the one involving Dr. Amira Camdzic? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you two or three questions regarding that part of your testimony in which you said that you took certain things out of apartments, loaded them onto trucks, transferred them to other places. Can you remember from which parts of the city you took out goods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would arrive at Centar I, Centar II, Bakina Luka, neighbourhoods like that. I know from other inmates the names of these neighbourhoods, but I myself cannot place them exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where would you drive those things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took things out of apartments or houses, loaded them onto trucks, and those goods were transported to Grude, Siroki Brijeg. I don't know about other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you did not accompany those things; you didn't unload them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the driver would say that there were people waiting to unload them at destination in Grude, Siroki Brijeg, and we would stay behind, wait for the truck to come back, and continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you know, the names of some of the soldiers who you recall as being there in those spots at the time on such occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of any prisoner who was working together with you? We can go into private session if necessary, if you want to tell us a name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could say a couple of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if we can go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, cross-examination, Mr. Meek? Cross-examined by Mr. Meek:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness PP. How are you this morning? Good morning. How are you? My name is Chris Meek, and I'm one of the lawyers for the accused Mr. Naletilic. I just have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, you have to turn off your mike because the witness is watching the lights, the red lights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness PP, at the time you were injured in March, the 16th of March, 1993, you were a soldier with the BH army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot hear anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness PP, can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness PP. My name is Chris Meek, and I'm one of the attorneys for the accused Naletilic. How are you this morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm fine, thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I understood your testimony yesterday, you were injured in the town of Gacko near Sarajevo on the 16th of March, 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't injured in Gacko. I was injured in Hrasnica, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, you were an active member of the BH army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me and the Trial Chamber what year you became a member of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became a member of the BH army on the 30th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you remained a member of the BH army continuously until this date today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we go into closed session -- private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness PP, you did not see any units from the Croatian army on the confrontation line, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not observe the presence of any HV or Croatian army units at your time at the confrontation line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian army -- there was a presence of the Croatian army at the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not at the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have occasion to see them on the confrontation line because I didn't spend much time there. I told you exactly where I had been, and I cannot say anything about things I'm not aware of. At the Heliodrom, there were units of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness PP. If you know, can you tell us what units you observed at the Heliodrom from the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several such units. I heard references to Tigers, the Split unit, the Rijeka unit. More of them were mentioned, more of those Croatian army units which were stationed or deployed at the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness PP, in your last answer, you said that you heard references to Tigers, the Split unit, and a third unit that were mentioned. Do I take it that you heard about these units but did never see them personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no contact with them, but I heard from inmates who had been out to work, that they had been to work with those Tigers and those others. I personally was not taken out to carry out works with any of those units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it, Witness PP, that you did not notice the presence of any of these Croatian army or HV in the Heliodrom premises personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not distinguish between the Split unit or the Rijeka unit and the Tiger unit. I wasn't -- I have never been down there. I can't say. All I know comes from the inmates who had been out to work with various units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 12th day of March, 1999, and also the 15th day of March, 1999, you said you did not notice the presence of HV in the Heliodrom premises. And that's the truth, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: If somebody had asked me, I might have answered. If nobody asked me, then I didn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher, please, to hand this to Witness PP?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness PP, the usher will hand you - in Croatian, your native language - your statement to the OTP from the days you were interviewed, on the 12th and 15th day of March, 1999, and I believe it's on page 3. I have highlighted the paragraph. And perhaps it's in the translation, but in the English translation, the last sentence - and I want you to tell this Trial Chamber whether this is correct - you stated: "I also didn't notice the presence of HV in the Heliodrom premises." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I said the same thing here just now. I said I had no contact with the Croatian army and all I know is from inmates who had such contact. I believe the meaning of this sentence is the same. I believe my testimony and my statement show no visible difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness PP, probably due to translation, it was my mistake and my misunderstanding. I have no further questions. I want to thank you for coming to this Tribunal to give your testimony, and I wish you the best in your future life. Thank you very much, PP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. No re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from Judges? Judge Clark? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Witness PP, can I ask you a few questions? When you would leave the Heliodrom to go and do the various days' work which we describe as forced labour, were you ever told in advance what work you were going to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And when did you actually find out what your tasks were? Was it when you had actually arrived at the site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we had arrived on the spot, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did the person who directed you towards this man Dinko or Vinko have a list who were to go in each truck -- or bus, I should say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the place where we were housed, Vinko or Dinko would come in, accompanied by two men, policemen or escorts. In any event, there were always two of them. He always had a list of people who had been out to work the previous day, and he would try to take the same people again, if they were able to work. Of course, to the same places where they had worked before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That, Witness PP, leads me to my next question. If the two men - there were always two, as you say - had a list each day of the people who had gone out the previous day, and as far as it was possible they selected that same list, did those two people, or any other people in their stead, check the list of detainees when you came home in the evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So the only check was in the morning. Well, could you assist the Trial Chamber by telling us what would happen if a name was called out and that person was unable to answer? Was there a series of questions to ascertain why he wasn't available?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When somebody wouldn't answer, they would ask what happened to that man, whether he had gotten killed or wounded on Santiceva Street or whether something else happened. That was the point of their questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And you say that the persons with the lists in the morning were, therefore, aware in your presence that from time to time, that prisoners who went out to do labour were actually killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. During the period that you were in the Heliodrom -- I know that you were fortunate enough to escape after two and a half months, but did you have any contact with any humanitarian organisation such as the Red Cross? Were you aware of their coming to the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They came to the camp, but I was not there at the time they came, because when they knew that the Red Cross people would come, they would transfer us to other places, so half of us would not be there, and half of us were actually not registered by the Red Cross. I happened to be in Sovici on one such occasion where the Red Cross came to register the detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: When you say that you were in Sovici when the Red Cross came, does that mean that the Red Cross were in Heliodrom while you were in Sovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you think that was an accident or a deliberate ploy on behalf of the authorities, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a deliberate ploy because it happened on several occasions. We could feel it whenever an international organisation was supposed to visit, such as the Red Cross. We knew because people were being taken away. For example, in a room where normally there would be 300 of us, only 10 or 20 people would remain. So it was on the basis of that that we were able to conclude that an international organisation such as the Red Cross was about to visit the camp. They wanted to have as few of us there as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. If I now ask you about this person who used to drive the blue bus, and you named the brand of bus, who you think -- whose name you think was either Dinko or Vinko. My understanding of your evidence in relation to his name was that he would tell you one day that his name was Dinko, and if you called him Dinko, he would say his name was Vinko. Do I understand you correctly on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: When did you find out, or how did you find out, or why do you believe that his last name was Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how he introduced himself. Whenever someone called him by the name of Dinko, he would say, "No, I'm not Dinko. I'm Vinko Martinovic," or the other way around. It was him who used those words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: If I can jump a little bit to the person who was your school friend and who you grew up with who was with the KB, the Convicts Battalion and who came to the hospital. I don't recall his name at the moment. Do you remember that man? It began with an "S." Do you remember you were telling us about this person who came to the hospital, and you knew him from your youth? Dzemo Skobalj.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dzemo, it's a man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. That's who I was talking about. I think you said you knew him because you had been to the same school together.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You were asked questions by Mr. Par on behalf Vinko Martinovic in relation to him. My understanding of what you said about him was that he told you that he was a member of the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And am I also correct that he told you that he was a member of a group called Stelici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: At that stage, did you know anything about the unit that was called after Stela's dog? Was that in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't know much. I had heard something, but I didn't know what the meaning of the word was. I was not familiar with that unit or with the man by the name of Stela until such time as -- when I experienced it personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was that after you had been taken away from the hospital and detained at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm really trying to establish, because it's not clear to me, at what stage you became aware that this former school friend of yours, Dzemo, was a member of the Convicts Battalion and then that he had any contact with a group called Stelici. At what stage did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in hospital, Dzemo came to see me with another man, with a friend of his who was actually the one who came to see me. But he happened to be with me at that time. And that is when I made contact with them, and they said that they were from the Convicts Battalion, that there was a unit by the name of Stelici, and something to that effect. That was the first time when I heard about them. And the second time I saw him was when he came to arrest me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: At what stage did you become aware of the connection between the Stelici and Mrmak, the name, as you told us, was, you believed, the name of Stela's dog? How did you hear that? How did you become aware, and when did you first become aware?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went out to perform labour, we spoke amongst ourselves, detainees, and there were a few of them who knew him personally, and they told us that that was his dog. I don't know whether it was Mrmak, Mrmat [phoen], or something like that. I cannot claim with certainty what the name was, but there was also an inscription of some sort on the insignia. But as I'm not 100 per cent sure, I'd rather not state it precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: If you're not 100 per cent sure of this, obviously I'll understand. It's a while ago. Can you recall if you had heard of the word "Mrmak" when you were still a patient in hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Is that no, you're not 100 per cent sure or no, you didn't hear about the name Mrmak when you were in hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about the name Mrmak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So can I understand your evidence to be that you did not hear the name Mrmak until after you had been taken from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went out to perform labour, I heard about Mrmak for the first time; I think it was when I was brought to work at the Bulevar. That was the first time that I came to do some work, and that was also the first time that I heard about Mrmak and Stelici, while I was doing that work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: While you were doing the work - some of it I appreciate was not actually in Mostar - but when you were in the town of Mostar and doing work, who did you understand as being the person in charge of the activities, the military activities, where you were brought?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm referring only to the work that you did near the Bulevar, near the confrontation line. So we can exclude when you were doing other works in various other parts of the country. Only in relation to the works near the confrontation line, did you have any idea who was the commander of the military activity in that limited area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stela. We were always told, "The boss is coming. Stela is coming. Stela is going to kill us all if you're not -- do the work properly," and things like that. So we knew it was Stela.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, if I bring you to what is probably a painful part of your evidence, it's the day on which you effected your escape, did you have any idea when you were taken out in the bus that morning that anything different was about to take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the moment we arrived at the spot, at the Health Centre, nothing unusual happened. But what happened after my escape, I don't know. There may have been other things that were taking place at the time, but I cannot tell you anything about them because I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, it was another day at work? When you were given the wooden rifle, where did it -- where did it come from? Did you see just one rifle, or were there a few of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw four rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was it immediately obvious to you that they were imitation rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, I appreciate that a prisoner in the presence of armed soldiers has few rights, but did any of you say anything or ask any questions? Because after all, this must have been a very unusual occurrence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one could muster enough courage to ask any questions whatsoever, because we knew that if we tried to oppose them in any way, they would squash us, they would kill us. They all had pistols. It was forced labour. There were no laws whatsoever. No one was responsible for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I have to ask you these details, because obviously this is painful for you. You talked about going down into the cellar on your own and when you got down there, Stela was at a desk, I think you said, with maps, and that there was a small man there. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was standing at the door, and people called him Dolma. Meanwhile, Stela was sitting at a desk inside. There was a map in front of him, and a chair near the desk, across the desk, and I sat on that chair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was this man Dolma - I know it's difficult to remember details like that - but was he wearing any sort of a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember very well. He had green trousers, which were commonly referred to as Vietnam trousers. He had a camouflage-patterned T-shirt and a black vest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: At what stage did the man who you described to us as Dado come into the frame?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dado approached me at the moment I was cleaning the rifles. He came to fetch me and take me to the basement where Stela was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think you described him as a big man with a beard, dark --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was he with you when you joined up with the other three detainees who were put into camouflage jackets and given wooden rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He then brought me back to them, and he showed me where we were supposed to go. He motioned to the building that we were supposed to reach and wait for them to cross over near that building. But after I passed the building in question, I no longer remember anything. I was wounded, but thank God I survived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You have been of great assistance to me, Witness PP. And thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge Clark's questions? Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have a couple of questions, Your Honours. Thank you very much. Further cross-examination by Mr. Par:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as regards the events which took place at the hospital involving Dzemo Skobalj, do you know that Vinko Martinovic, Stela, used to be the commander of a unit during the war with Serbs, a unit which was not within the HVO? Are you familiar with that fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear that Vinko Martinovic was a commander of an HOS unit, but again, this is something that I heard, that he was one of the commanding persons with HOS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were his soldiers at that time also referred to as Stelici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HOS, did it -- was it disbanded at some point in time as a military formation before the war between -- opposing Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was disbanded before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you think that it is possible -- speaking of the period of time before the conflict opposing Muslims and Croats, and before the formation of Stela's unit, was it possible for members of his previous unit to be referred to as Stelici? Did they recognise themselves as Stelici? So would it be possible for someone else other than the members of this unit to be -- the Vinko Skrobo unit to be called -- to be referred to as Stelici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm really sorry, but I have to tell you something. I know that you are defending Stela for money. But I have come here to tell the Court the truth, and I have to tell you everything I know about Stela.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Just another very brief question regarding command at the separation line. You said that you knew that Stela was the commander because he would visit you to inspect the situation. Do you mean that he was only in charge of the Health Centre, or other areas as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I'm not very familiar with the area itself because a few metres further, there would be another street with another name. I know the area was referred to as "the Bulevar," and I know that this is where we performed labour, and this is where Stela was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. A few questions. Further examination by Mr. Bos:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness PP, you were asked about these lists -- in the morning when you would be picked up from the Heliodrom, that people would come with a list, and that sometimes people who would be called out from the list were no longer there. My question is: How often would that happen that people were not there, prisoners were not there who were called out from the list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it also happen that witnesses who were called out would not be able to come because they were injured? Prisoners, I'm sorry. I said "witnesses," but I meant prisoners.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already answered the question. Sometimes the detainee would be killed or taken away or not be -- to work elsewhere and not be returned to the Heliodrom, so there were always people who were missing, those who had left in the morning. Not everybody would return to the same spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for helping us by giving your evidence. When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of the room. We wish you good luck in the future.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to tender into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have two exhibits that need to be tendered. One is Exhibit 888, which is the sketch made by the witness. And I would like to tender that under seal because his name appears on the sketch. And the other exhibit is 14.11, which the witness marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections? Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So those two documents are admitted into the evidence. And Document P888 is under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document P888 is now PP888, and it is under seal. Exhibit P14.11 is PP14.11/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that D1/35, which was a picture that Witness OO marked on the -- marked the direction that the tank was moving yesterday, or the day before, be admitted, please. D1/35, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Excuse me, are you referring to this witness, Witness PP?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness OO, I think. It's OO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it is admitted into evidence, for Witness OO, not for Witness PP.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That Exhibit D1/35 is now DD1/35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you ready for your next witness, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Scott will take the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next witness will be a protected witness. He will be asking for a pseudonym and voice and face distortion, and if granted, of course, that may take some few minutes to set that up.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Victims and Witness Section informed me that the witness is on his way. He should be here in the next five minutes or so, because we need to prepare for the voice distortion, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any objections for those protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: None from the Defence of Mr. Naletilic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We are adjourned for ten minutes. We will resume at 20 to 11.00. --- Break taken at 10.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott, would you please brief us about the relevance in the indictment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour. May it please the Court, the testimony of this witness will relate to the background part of the indictment, paragraphs 7 and 11; the matters of superior authority, paragraphs 14, 15, and 16; general allegations, paragraphs 18, 19, and 20; count 1, persecutions, paragraph 27 and 28, paragraph 30, paragraph 33 and 34; counts 2 through 5, paragraphs 35 through 38, 40, 44; and counts 9 through 12, paragraphs 45 and 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, would you please stand up? Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I thought I might inquire, since it's already ten to 11.00, might the Chamber allow us to take the witness for approximately half an hour and take the break a bit later? It doesn't really matter, but we will barely get started now and then it will be time for the break. But whichever the Court prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may proceed. We might stop at 11.20. How about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That would be helpful, I think. Thank you very much. Examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, good morning. Your request for protective measures has been granted, which means that you will be given what's called a pseudonym, essentially a letter or series of letters that will be used to identify you for purposes of the record, and your true name will not be used in court and will not be put on the record, to protect your identification. Further, you will be granted what's called facial image distortion so that in any sort of broadcast of these proceedings, your face will not be shown, again to protect your identity. And finally, your voice will also be protected. For purposes of these protections, let me alert you that, especially concerning the voice distortion, I will have to turn off my microphone after I finish asking you a question and then you will give your answer. Now, since we don't -- you and I do not speak the same language that normally will probably not be a problem because there is usually a lag in translation in any event, but nonetheless, I caution you about that and so you will understand. Now, for these reasons, Witness, you have been given the pseudonym, which is QQ, and that is how you will be referred to in court, not only by me but by Defence counsel and by the Judges, should they have questions for you. Now, I'm going to have the usher show you a piece of paper, and I simply want to you say - and for all the reasons I've just said, don't state your name, but just say - is that your name on that piece of paper; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Usher, if that could be displayed in the courtroom, please. Mr. President, I'm going to take the first series of questions and try to do as much as possible at the beginning of this witness's testimony in private session in order to stay out of private session as much as possible. So if we could go to private session for a few minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, we've come up to about the 8th of May. You've told us you were stopped the day before. On the 8th of May, will you take your story forward. What happened on the 8th of May? Were you allowed to go on your way, or what happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: On the 8th of May, all passengers were ordered to board the bus. It must have been an agreement with the army. We took the road which was called the Put Spasa route, or "the salvation route," and we were stopped by the army police at one point in time. Eleven of us able-bodied men were taken out. They didn't allow us to take our things. I still had some money on me in my trousers. And we were put on a van and taken to the elementary school in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've said just now that - looking at the transcript - that the army police stopped you and took 11 of you off the bus. Can you further identify these army police, what type of police they were, and if you can tell us, which army were they part of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: The military police belonged to the HVO. We could see it written, "HVO." And they had, of course, the typical white belts and pump-action rifles. Some had Kalashnikovs as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For geographic reference, when you were stopped at that time, was this around a place that used to be called Tomislavgrad, and since then the name has changed to Duvno?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: No, no, no, it used to be called Duvno, and the name has been changed to Tomislavgrad. Yes, we were stopped not far from there near a lake. It was the first time I saw that lake. I think it's a natural lake. There was a cottage house there and a swing gate on the road where they stopped private vehicles, buses, everyone. But it was not very far from Tomislavgrad. It didn't take us very long to reach the town from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you then taken to any particular location or building where you were held further?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: We were taken to an abandoned school building, to the basement of that school. I think it was an elementary school or a secondary school. I'm not sure. I never asked, and I didn't know. And there were already 40 or 50 people there, various people, including drivers, who were transporting various goods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that as opposed to the first group of people you told us about a few minutes ago, this group of men in the school at Duvno -- group of prisoners, excuse me -- at the elementary school in Duvno, that these were military-aged men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: They were all military-age men, but there were a few elderly people as well. There was also a woman, but the police treated her correctly. They let her go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were the men, including yourself, treated during this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: They didn't treat us very well. They were quite dangerous, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how long you were kept at this location, that is, the school in Duvno, or Tomislavgrad, however you identify it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: I was there for 15 days - I have documents to prove it - together with 10 other people. Eleven of us were there for 15 days, and others stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the -- who appeared to you, perhaps, to be the commander, or the person in charge of this detention facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: I remember that an individual by the name of Tomo was there. He was a very nice person. He held the rank of major, and I learned that Glasnovic was the main commander in Tomislavgrad. I saw him only on one occasion. He was a rather fine, polite gentleman, just as Tomo, who was one of the commanders. He didn't let us work too hard at Kupres, at Cuke, when we were taken there to do some work. So I really cannot make any complaint about these gentlemen. However, others came from elsewhere who beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can just finish with one or two clarifying questions, then perhaps we could take the break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you just told us - and that was my next question - during the approximate 15 days that you were held at this location, were you taken to perform labour at one or more locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: All of us were taken to do forced labour. We were taken to the front line and made to dig trenches and communication trenches. All of us had to go and dig trenches. However, I should say once again that they were more or less fair. They didn't force us in a brutal way, especially when I told them I had been at the Croatian front. He would bring me beer or coffee. Once again, I have to say that they were nice people. But there was a group of people who came to beat us, a gang of men, people who used to be members of the HOS, which was a paramilitary formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I suggest we can stop there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll resume at quarter to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness QQ, before the break, you said that while some of the people at the school treated you and the other prisoners well, or fairly, at least, that there were others who came to the school who abused or mistreated you and other prisoners. Can you tell us the names or about any particular incidents in which that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Well, I can. I remembered in particular one young man whose name was Dugonjic, an evil man, very dangerous, who beat us very badly. I had been a karate man for a while, and I can take hits, but this was bad beating. He tied me once to my bed and hit me with clubs, with his hands. They took people out as well. I noticed that on one occasion, two or three men were missing, and there were traces of blood in the room. In the morning, I noticed that an attempt was made to wash it off. But in the morning, we didn't dare comment. We kept quiet, though. It was Croat against Croat. I was disappointed. One man came and asked us to tell how we were mistreated, and we told him. There were also young men who were found guilty of theft, and they were kept separately. They were allowed to beat us too. That's what I can tell you, as far as Tomislavgrad is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This man named Dugonjic, what --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: That was his nickname or his last name. I don't know that. I remembered that man very well. Other people came too, such as one Robi. I found out he was from Siroki Brijeg or Citluk. He also beat us badly. He broke two of my ribs once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, one further final question on Dugonjic, and then I'll go forward to Robi. Can you identify what military unit or formation that Mr. Dugonjic was part of, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: He wore a white belt too, and he had two or three HVO badges with the sign of crossed rifles, and all of them were mixed, HOS, HVO, HV, until a conflict arose. There was another Tomo, a nice man, who knew me and protected me. He gave me some bandages and cloth to put on my broken ribs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness, I'm going to stop you there. When you mentioned the fact that he wore a white belt, was that an indication to you of someone being military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Certainly. Even in Tito's time, the military police, the current one and the past one, they always wore white belts. Everyone knows that, even children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned already that other soldiers, other persons, would come to the -- this location, this facility, and be allowed -- or at least -- strike that. And beat prisoners. My question is: Do you know how it is that they were allowed access to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, you see, it was chaos. Everybody tried to cheat everybody, to control more territory, to have more place for looting. I don't know how they entered the school building, but they would come in drunk and beat people for kicks, and they took out their anger for all -- for their lost loved ones on us. I can resist, and I can hold my own in a fight, but I was tied down, and sometimes they beat me so bad that I couldn't take it any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you go back to this man Robi. How did you know him or come to know him, and what did he do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: He beat us the most, together with Dugonjic. Once when I lost consciousness and fell on the ground, somebody told Robi, "Leave him alone. Let him die." I can tell you a lot about this Robi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know at that time or come to know the military unit that he was part of, this Robi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes. I learned later that he was from the Convicts Battalion, the KB.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you learn that? What do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: I saw him at Siroki Brijeg. I also saw him in Mostar. I am good at remembering faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The times when this Robi beat you, was he asking you questions or trying to get information from you, or did you have any understanding why it was that he was treating you in this way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: I noticed there was no purpose to it. He was beating me just because I was a Muslim. He said, "You Muslims, what are you doing to us?" He would come in drunk. He had no -- not a humane bone in him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Witness QQ, I want to move us forward a bit. After this about 15 days when you were held at the school, were you and some of the other prisoners then moved to another detention facility in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes. A nice young man took the 11 of us who had been taken off the bus, he took us in this van and gave us food. I cannot remember his name. I don't think he told us. He turned us over to the Ljubuski prison. It's an old prison; I noticed by the door. So he took us to Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Ljubuski, were there other prisoners already there? I'm not asking you for any names right now, just saying did you find there were already prisoners there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: There are many, many people from Mostar, many people who were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: I know a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we go to private session for a moment or two?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness QQ, can you give us an approximate number of how many prisoners were moved to Heliodrom with you about that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Well, approximately 300 or more. Perhaps even 500. There were five or four buses and trucks that transported the people. I was in one of the trucks. Say if one bus can carry 50 passengers under normal circumstances, this time they would load up to 100 people. And we were promised to be released. That is what they told us, that they were going to release us -- I'm sorry, to exchange us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you, in fact, released or exchanged at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Of course not. We ended up in a much worse camp to the Heliodrom, at Rodoc, where this ex-air force unit was -- used to be located, next to a metal factory. It was a military barracks at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find, either among the men that you were -- the persons that you were moved with from Ljubuski to the Heliodrom or at the Heliodrom - and you can assist us with any clarification - did you find that a number of those men were from Zepce?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: You mean Muslims? The detainees?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: There were two or three from Zepce. Later on, other buses arrived carrying 150 people, thereabouts. I know quite a few of those people. They were from the village of Lug, near the village of Zepce, that had been taken over by Croats, and also the village of Vrbica. They were transported through the Serb territory via Teslic. There must have been an agreement between Croats and Serbs. They were attacking the town of Zavidovici and captured those two villages. So they rounded up all able-bodied men and loaded them onto buses and took them to Ljubuski and Dretelj, and from Dretelj to the Heliodrom. They took them to various places. I know quite a few people from that group. But there were three men from Zepce with me in my group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness, just a couple of follow-up questions on that. Were you able to determine during the time you were held, were all of these men from Zepce? Both the ones you travelled with and the ones who were brought -- you say that were brought there to Heliodrom later, do you know whether they were all ABiH soldiers or were they citizens -- excuse me, private citizens, or what did you know of their status, if anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: I know the situation very well. There were elderly people there, very young people as well. They were all civilians. No one was wearing any uniform. And they told me that they were not members of the army. There were a lot of people in -- living in Zavidovici, and I'm familiar with the situation in Zepce. They didn't have to mobilise everyone. They had enough able-bodied men. So they told me that they had not been captured at the front lines but at their homes. And they wanted to actually have as many people as possible in various camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my next question before moving on: You said in order to be moved from Zepce in this way, that these buses or however -- the vehicles they were transported in had to cross through Serb territory. Do you know how that was possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We went --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object, although I hate to interrupt my learned colleague in his examination, but I do not understand what the relevance of Zepce is for the indictment and the population of Zepce. How relevant is it for our case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott? What's the relevance in the indictment for this particular question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's relevant in a couple of respects, and I really am almost done. In fact, with this last question, I am done with the questions. It's not something I had any intention to spend a great deal of time on. The relevance is - and part of what we are required to prove - is that these things that were happening were part of a widespread and systematic practices. They were not unique simply to the Mostar area or even Jablanica and the other areas but extended so far away as Zepce, which is in North-Central Bosnia, and many prisoners in our case -- we submit, in our case, in a systematic and widespread way were being collected from all over Bosnia and taken to such places as the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What I mean is that particular question. The question is that the vehicles they were transported in had to cross through Serb territories. Do you know how that was possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the witness may know or may not know, but what's the relevance to this issue? Are you suggesting that even Serbia is involved in this case, so as to prove that the international armed conflict happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not suggesting it for purposes of international armed conflict. I think the Judges, Your Honours, have heard, and I suspect you may hear more in the future, about fighting with the Serbs and how many of these things were justified by the fact that they were fighting against the Serbs, et cetera, and there has been past discussion of that in cross-examination. And the Prosecution case has been, and will be -- that at least in some respects, not all respects, but in a number of significant respects throughout this relevant time period, in fact, the Serbs and the Croats in these areas were not, in fact, fighting and, in fact, were operating quite jointly on numerous occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We don't believe this question is relevant to the case we are now hearing. Would you please skip this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to the Heliodrom, sir, just give us -- what did you find there and how were you treated in a general way? I'll ask you some specifics, but what did you find when you got to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: When we got to the Heliodrom, having left from Siroki Brijeg, we found many prisoners there, including elderly people, women, and children. We were lined up in two rows on an asphalt area. The military police of the HVO distributed us in various places. I learned that it was some kind of Central Military Prison. Some people were put up in school buildings, sports halls. Every single corner of the complex was packed with people that they were rounding up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We don't get any translation. Would you please try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether I understand correctly what has been said here in the record. I see the words "having left from Siroki Brijeg." Are we talking about two events, the arrival at Ljubuski, because we're following the witness in the Croatian language? Can that be clarified, please? Of course, I can take it up during the cross-examination, because I believe that we're talking about the events Ljubuski and then Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: To me, it's quite clear. But anyway, Mr. Scott, would you please clear it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you've probably heard the exchanges in the last moment. In your answer just now, you said, when you got to Heliodrom, "having left from Siroki Brijeg." Now, we are going to talk about Siroki Brijeg in the course of your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: No, not Siroki Brijeg, but Ljubuski. We were taken from Ljubuski to the Heliodrom. It was only later on that I went to Siroki Brijeg. You asked me about the place that we were transferred from; that is, we were transferred from Ljubuski to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you're absolutely right, and thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: To the barracks of the aviation of the ex-JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you -- and I'm talking now about --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: I know I speak very fast. I apologise. It's just the natural way I speak. But I'll try and do my best and slow down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the approximate first month that you were at the Heliodrom, were you used to perform forced labour in a number of locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did a lot of forced labour. I spent a lot of time at the Heliodrom. That month, we spent a lot of time digging trenches around the barracks in various ditches, but we were also taken to other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time, after a few weeks, that you were assigned to work in the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes. There were four or five Orthodox people there, Serbs. One was from Prijedor but was eventually exchanged. He was wearing a uniform. But since many soldiers knew me, I was sort of protected, and I was sent to the kitchen to work there. So I spent quite some time working as a cook there and distributing food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that regard, were you involved in taking food to other prisoners in a number of locations even outside the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes. I would take food two or three times outside the Heliodrom, some daily rations, things like that. There was a soldier whose name I don't want to mention who sometimes came with me. Once we went to the Hum mountain above Mostar. I remember distributing food to the soldiers there. I remember I had a hangover that day. I went to one of the dugouts there and sat down with them. I didn't emphasise that in my statement. Anyway, there are so many things that I didn't mention in my statement. I never thought that I would be called here to testify. It's not that I really wanted to come. But anyway, I came here to speak up. I haven't come because of myself but because of others who have died. I have lived in over 20 countries. I used to like to work, and I Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts – Pages 6203 to 6211. used to like people in general. But things happened the way they did. There's nothing I can do about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness QQ, thank you for that. Let me ask you about one particular location. Did you ever have to take food to some place called the mechanical engineering faculty in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Not directly from the Heliodrom. This soldier gave me some of it. We went to the university building . I don't know which university it was - he went to university; I think he was an engineer - since I had never been in Mostar before the war and I don't know Mostar very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet any sort of an HVO officer at this - I'll just say your term - at the university at this time when you delivered food there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: I used to meet a lot of officers. I met Mr. Stela. I knew him. He had some kind of headquarters there, red building whose name I don't know. I wasn't interested in that. Yes, I did meet quite a few of them, including Tuta on a couple of occasions. I knew several of those officers. I would meet them from time to time. But not many of them openly displayed any rank, because they were trying to keep them secret. Stela was a colonel by rank at that time, and he said that we should respect him as a colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, Witness QQ, let me come back to these men in a few minutes. Did you ever meet a person named Juka Prazina at the university location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I did. Sorry, I forgot him. Now, that's an evil man, a Muslim, but an evil man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber any exchange or conversation you might have had with Mr. Prazina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Prazina beat the Muslims more than HVO soldiers did. He was the worst. He quarrelled with the BH army and was leading an independent brigade. He had a conflict with Vehbija Karic, a colonel of the BH army at the Mount Igman. A relative of mine used to be a major in the old army, and I learned many such things from him. He was later on transferred to Salakovac, to the checkpoint there. He was very soon transferred and went over to Juka's unit. He was also a colonel. He was addressed by other people as a colonel. And such people received very often promotion during this war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me take you back to this Mr. Juka. My question to you was: Do you remember having any conversation with Juka at the time you saw him around the university?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: He wasn't quite accessible. Juka Prazina didn't like to talk to Muslims very much. He didn't want us to approach him. He came to the Heliodrom on several occasions and beat people, but I have to be -- I have to tell the truth: He didn't beat me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know at that time or come to learn about any relationship that Juka had with the man called Tuta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm objecting to the leading of the witness in a way which really warrants a vigorous objection on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can't very well ask this man to go through a long list of names of everyone he spoke to. I have to direct him somehow to the pertinent part of his testimony. I didn't try to suggest anything specific, other than mention a name in order to guide the witness's testimony in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, at this stage, we come upon the names of the accused, so I want you to be very careful to avoid any leading questions in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Let me rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you knew Juka Prazina. Did you come to know --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come to know of what military formation he was part of and any other officers that he was associated with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: The Convicts Battalion, of course, with Tuta, Stela, many other HVO officers. He was quick as a cat. He could be seen at various places, here and there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, and who is the "he" you're referring to now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, sir -- just now, you said, "He was quick as a cat. He could be seen at various places."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Juka, Juka, Juka Prazina. Sorry. Sorry. I didn't express myself well. Juka Prazina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when you were registered -- visited and registered by the Red Cross at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes. On the 3rd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can have the usher's assistance please. I think we have them here still. There are two exhibits I'd like to be provided to the witness, P889 and P752.2. We have copies. For the Registrar, 889 and 752.2. And I'll ask that they not be put on the ELMO and that they be received under seal because they will identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Are these new exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe they may be, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have a copy, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Usher? Mr. President, I was just waiting to see that the booths had been provided. I think I see that they have, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if I can direct your attention, first of all, to P889. Again I'm going to caution you not to say anything about your name, but can you confirm and -- obviously looking at the original document attached, if you turn to the second page, can you tell the Chamber what that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: This is an identity card of the Red Cross. It has two parts. One part is what they get to keep, and the other part is for us. We had to sign this other part, and it is all the -- all of the data are entered into a computer which is based in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say you recall being registered on approximately the 3rd of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes, on the 3rd of June, yes, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look at the next document, 752.2, and tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: This one here -- sorry, what this is, this is a letter from the Red Cross in Geneva. I was given this in Zagreb as I got out, and got the certificate from Tuta that I could be released on the 16th of February, 1994. So I went there to ask them for this official letter, because other international organisations needed it. I had to have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I have no more questions about those documents, so you can put those to one side. Did you come to know some of the leading guards or commanders at the Heliodrom during the time that you were detained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes, quite a few of them. Quite a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name some of them, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: There was a guy by the name of Ante Smiljanic, and as far as I could tell he was one of -- he was a guard command of this military police, people who guarded us. Buhovac. Then Miro Marjanovic, an ugly guy. Then there was a Boro, Boro Saba, something like that. I remember him as well. Then another one by the name of Skender, or nicknamed Skender, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in naming those particular ones, what is it about them that causes them to stick in your memory, perhaps more than others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: They ran this camp. They said something to the effect that I was finding other people -- they were taking gold. There were a lot of people who used to work abroad, like myself, in Germany, Iraq even, and they brought me a crate of beer and they brought me some roasted pork. They asked me if I ate pork, and I told them that I was a Hindu, that I could eat anything when I'm hungry. He said, "Could the two of us do business?" That's what Smiljanic, Boro said. I said, "What kind of business?" He said, "These guys who are with you, are they willing to pay each 10.000 German marks for me to take them to the border at Bregana? Perhaps they have family or relatives in Germany. I will call them from Zagreb. We can make contact. They -- all they have to do is bring the money." And that's how many people were released and taken away. And he promised me that I would be released if I bring him a lot of such people. There was a young man from Travnik. It's not important who he really is, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not want to interrupt you earlier, but again, let us come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It is something, Mr. President, the Chamber will hear more about, but I think better a bit later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In talking about these men that you've named a few moments ago - Smiljanic, Buhovac, Marjanovic - how did they treat the prisoners at the Heliodrom, in your experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Badly, badly. There were some nice guys, I have to say, but I don't want to give you their names, members of the military police, people who gave us some food to eat, some modest food, rice and lentils. I lost 23 kilos in those days. However, others were very bad, and they treated us badly. Miro Marjanovic, for instance. He was a dangerous guy, very, very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I direct you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: They caused a lot of trouble.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apology, there was a pause in translation. I thought it was finished. I'm sorry. Let me direct your attention to -- in the building or around the location where you were held, were there some solitary cells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: There were at least ten solitary cells, partitioned, prepared in advance, with metal doors and tin installed beforehand. Downstairs there was a kitchen. There were even two or three women in solitary confinement. There were a lot of people there, all kinds of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you off for a moment before you name a lot of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I ask that the last line or two please be redacted, and then can we go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will redact those two lines, and we will go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in the open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness QQ, I don't want you to name any names or give any particular details at the moment but just respond generally to this question: The women that you knew to be prisoners at the Heliodrom that you've named, and generally speaking, in the last few minutes, do you know whether they were sexually mistreated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify any of the HVO soldiers who were - again, I'm not going to ask you for any specific incidents - but some of the HVO soldiers who were involved in that activity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Miro Marijanovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I've let this go on for some time, but this is not within the scope of the indictment. These are not allegations which have been specifically alleged. We are surprised about this testimony, and I object. It's just not relevant. The probative value is so far outweighed by the prejudicial effect that the accused cannot receive a fair trial if this kind of evidence is going to be coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, I have to tell you that you have two counsels on your team. Only one should deal with one witness mainly. The second thing, we don't know whether it's really relevant or not to this very case, but we would like to hear the answer from this witness. Witness, you may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question that I last put to you, Witness, was: Can you identify any of the HVO soldiers who were involved in sexually mistreating the women prisoners, the female prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Ante Smiljanic, Miro Marijanovic. They were vicious. They had an understanding. They had a room downstairs where they took women, taking turns. I peeped through a keyhole. I was curious. Any woman who didn't want to go into that room, solitary confinement room, got a slap on the face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness, I'm not going to pursue that further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was trying to take it very generally, and that's as far as I will take it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Chamber, please, did you ever come across a man who was being held at the Heliodrom during this time? He was an imam called Mezet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Mezet, yes, there was Mezet. There was Ahmet Biber. There were several imams. Mezet was from Rodoc. He had two sons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to the Imam Mezet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: On two occasions, they took him out and beat him up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Because he took a second helping. That was not allowed. He cheated and got a second helping. That's why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention, please, to the latter part of July 1993. Were you taken from the Heliodrom to perform forced labour about that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken to do a lot of forced labour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you recall about that day in particular? What I'd like you to do, sir, on this -- because I don't want to lead -- what lawyers might call lead you through this too much, except to give you the opportunity to say what happened on that day. If you can just start with the beginning of the day. You were taken from the Heliodrom into Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: They took us down to Santiceva Street, the Bulevar. I remember those streets. There were several trucks full of people. Some dug trenches. Some filled bags. Some covered walls and made holes in the walls so that HVO soldiers can easily pass from room to room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see -- well, where did you go during that morning, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: That morning, I was told that I needed to help some people carry some packages. And I found myself in the middle of all that commotion. I was forced to go dig trenches, fortify the line. There were a lot of works that needed doing. I didn't have time to eat or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come across a prisoner named Zikro Karso?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object to the question and to what follows, considering that a man and an incident are concerned who have absolutely no relevance to the indictment. It is disputable whether this person existed at all. We are now supposed to hear about another alleged murder which does not feature in the indictment. It is mentioned nowhere in the indictment. And I believe it is another attempt to create a false image in order to mislead the Trial Chamber. It is our case that this event never happened, and it is described nowhere in the indictment, nor is anything of the sort alleged by the Prosecutor when he enumerated the counts in the indictment that this witness will cover. I would appreciate it very much if we could remain within the scope of the indictment. THE WITNESS [Interpretation] Can I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, we also have some questions concerning the series of questions. First of all, you asked about the later days of July; then you mentioned about a certain date. But we don't know what is the specific date of that day this incident happened. So you might clear it up for us. Secondly, could you give us some explanation about the questioning of that prisoner named Zikro Karso? You have to understand the Defence counsel will put their case in their defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President. I did -- I will come back to the date, and I wanted to give, frankly, the witness the opportunity to say the date as much as possible himself, but I will ask him to clarify it as much as he can. In terms of the question, this series of questions, first off, Mr. President, this -- there has been fair notice for all the reasons we've discussed before about the nature of the allegations in the indictment. This account is also clearly stated and described in the 65 ter witness summaries that were provided to counsel a long time ago. So this comes as no surprise to anyone. Thirdly, what this witness -- what I expect this witness to say, based on prior statements, is that this very -- reflects very much on Mr. Martinovic, not because he personally killed this man - and it will not be our position - but that he was present, that this was carried out by one of his subordinates and he saw it happen, did nothing to prevent it, did nothing to punish it, and that's directly related to his being a superior who failed to prevent or punish acts of his subordinates. It's directly relevant to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
