utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I not only object to the question, I also protest against what the Prosecutor just said because he has begun to testify himself. Of course we got summaries of statements of all witnesses, but they don't mean anything to us. They give us no warning at all. Mr. President, Your Honours, not in a single count of the indictment is this event mentioned, not even the date, not even the man. At no point have we been warned that this witness will be testifying today about this matter. Mr. President, we have always had the opportunity to use some sort of special defence and claim that our client was in a different place at the time. So he could have defended himself by alibi or otherwise. But today, we don't have that possibility because we don't have this in the indictment. If it's not in the indictment, then why should something be imposed on us out of the blue as a new problem? How are we to defend ourselves? How are we to conduct the cross? The fact that the Prosecutor provided us with statements including references to this incident means nothing until the witness comes here to testify live, in voce. It is an aperto capite, this time again. This has been happening to us all the time in this case, from the video, from some witnesses who speak about events which have nothing to do with us. What are we to defend ourselves from? After two-thirds of the evidence and witnesses have been presented, we only now find out that we are just to begin defending ourselves, just to begin conducting our investigations in order to defend ourselves from these facts. We are only now learning about this incident. If you allow this, Honourable Judges, if you allow examination regarding a murder which I claim de facto and de jure is inadmissible, then I kindly ask you, please, give us a deadline for appeal, for clarification. Give us some time to investigate where our client was at that moment. Charge it so that we can defend ourselves. This way, I really don't know what to do. I, as Defence counsel, I had to question my own integrity as an attorney at law, as Defence counsel. I am beginning to think that I'm not in a position to defend my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not the first time that the Defence is addressing the Trial Chamber in its impotence, helplessness. I absolutely share the view of my colleague, and we are now seriously discussing how to go on with this defence, and we are exchanging views with our clients as well, and between us. What are we to do if this is going to continue? This Tribunal should set the standard in the legal world, instead of putting us in the situation in which we are today. And we are truly thinking, as my colleague Seric said, that perhaps we ought to simply give all this up. We are being watched by the entire world. The judgement will become history tomorrow. We are learning new rules every day from various legal systems. We cannot go on unprepared. We really can't. We are being told that everything has been given to us in advance. That's not true. This witness is saying things, half of which are not in his statement. You know very well that we are doing our homework, Honourable Judges. You know that we are doing our best to keep within the schedule, to meet our obligations towards the clients, to honour our code of ethics, but we really cannot go on this way any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I have to say that I will guarantee you that you will have full opportunity to defend your client in a later stage on this very issue. If you could have alibi on this case, we are very glad to hear this witness in the future. There is another thing I want to make sure, which is that -- whether this incident is properly informed to the Defence counsel in a timely manner. I think that's the very issue we are going to discuss about, so that to allow the Defence counsel to have enough time to prepare their case. We should avoid any surprise attack or pre-emptive attack before this trial. Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I hear a lot of noise, but it has nothing to do with the facts or the law applicable to this situation. The indictment is clear. We have discussed this point before. This is something that has come up, as the Chamber well knows now, over the last several weeks. It was discussed extensively again yesterday or the day before in connection with the paragraphs of the indictment which I read to the Chamber at that time. Those exacts same paragraphs clearly apply here, and other paragraphs in the indictment as well. There has been complete and fair notice. It is apparently counsel's view that the jurisprudence of the Tribunal would require an indictment to essentially be a bill of evidence. We would have to put out -- we would have to list every incident, every witness, every -- we would have to put out our evidence in the indictment, to prove such things as superior authority, to prove such things as notice, to prove a course and pattern of conduct by which this accused -- these accused clearly knew that these things were taking place, and not only did they know, but they turned a blind eye and a deaf ear to these things over and over and over again. Now, I do not believe that is the jurisprudence of this institution. That would turn an indictment into hundreds of pages of documents, listing every --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. Every incident, every witness, every document, every exhibit that we intend to put in to prove our case. Now, just as counsel apparently the other day had not read the indictment, they apparently have not recently read the 65 ter summaries as well. 65 ter summaries were filed more than a year ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Scott, before you go on to that, I don't have the indictment with me. That's not an issue. Could you direct me to a count in the indictment which uses the word "killings"? Just remind me of that. I'm sorry I don't have the indictment with me. I usually do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour. Just a moment please. First of all, Your Honour, it's in a number of places, but starting with counts 2 through 8 and the very paragraphs I referred the Chamber to earlier. Paragraphs 35 through 44, all touch on these matters. And the specific counts, to answer Your Honour Judge Clark's question, are: Count 6, murder, crime against humanity; count 7, wilful killing, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions; and count 8, murder, a violation of the laws or customs of war. There are also killing counts, if you will, in count 13, count 14, and count 15. I believe those, Your Honours, are the counts that mention that. Mr. President, the 65 -- what this institution does have is, after asking for a concise indictment, there are a number of disclosure rules. One of those is 65 ter, which requires plainly that the Prosecution, and at the appropriate time the Defence, state its case and state -- give further outlines of the evidence for these very purposes, not that would be in the indictment but that would be in other documents related to the case. More than one year ago, when Judge Wald was still the Pre-Trial Judge in this case, the Prosecution filed 65 ter witness summaries. I don't have those in front of me at the moment, but I am fairly confident that this matter was specifically disclosed as to this witness. I don't want to state with certainty, because I don't want to give the Court more assurance than I properly should, without having the document in front of me. I do have in front of me, however, the document that was filed, the amended 65 ter list of witnesses, filed on the 16th of August of 2001. I direct the Chamber - and again, I will not, of course, mention the witness's name - but to page 55 and 56 of those summaries. And the Chamber will quite plainly see that exactly this incident is described in the top part of the box on page 56. There has been complete notice, probably more than a year ago, certainly since August, and I'm afraid that, again, counsel sometimes just makes claims and representations to the Chamber that just simply aren't true. The document is there. If I've misread something, I please invite everyone, perhaps during the lunch hour, Mr. President -- those summaries can be reviewed. And again, I direct the Chamber's particular attention to page 55 and 56, and I think you will see that it is there in black and white. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we are a few minutes past the time. We will resume at 2.30 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.03 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We apologise for the delay. Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you for allowing me to address the Chamber, in particular in view of the allegations made by the Prosecutor. At the outset, let me just state that there seems to have been an incident, if I may call it that way, because prior to leaving the courtroom, the witness turned to the accused and showed him his tongue. And then my client replied by asking him, "Are you afraid of God -- aren't you afraid of God?" I'm just telling you this because I don't want anything happening in this courtroom over which we wouldn't have any control. During the break, I really tried to concentrate myself as best as I could so that I can make my statement now in a most impartial and disinterested way. I have to respond to what my learned colleague has stated prior to the break. It is true, Mr. President, that we received witness statements well ahead of time and that we had sufficient time for us to take all that material into account. However, at the moment we receive such material, such statements, we are not in a position to know whether the Prosecutor -- and such things have already happened in the past and now we are nearing the end of Prosecutor's case. We will be working until two weeks after the New Year's eve. What I'm saying is that the Prosecutor, by leading the witness through the examination-in-chief, sometimes skipped large portions of their statements. So at the moment we receive the statements, we do not know which parts of the statements would eventually be used at trial and on which parts of the statement he will eventually base his examination-in-chief. So the result of the examination-in-chief, the final examination-in-chief will constitute the basis on which you make your findings, Your Honour. So I do admit that we did receive the statement of this witness. However, in situation when we do not know what the Prosecutor intends to skip and what he intends to use as the basis of his examination-in-chief, I must say that this is, formally speaking, the first time for us that we become aware of such events. In addition to the objections that we had to the indictment, we strongly object to some very vague allegations. My learned friend from the Prosecution has stated the relevant paragraphs and relevant counts, such as the count -- counts 2 to 8, unlawful labour and human shields, and inhumane treatment or willful killing, persecution and willful causing of great suffering. We have in counts 13 to 17 -- so in addition to these crimes, we also have murder in counts 13 to 17. When the Prosecutor is alleging the legal term of "murder" in respect of which he wishes to examine this witness, he is not referring to the proper legal qualification of the act, which is required if we wish to speak of the murder as a crime in the indictment as it is stated in counts 13 to 17. For example, in count 13 to 17, we have the name of the victim, we have the specific date, and we have the specific event. And this was specifically charged in the indictment by the Prosecutor. So that is one example. However, we have had several cases, including what happened today, when Prosecutor stated that there were so many victims that it was simply impossible for him to enumerate in the indictment all of their names. I could, perhaps, agree with that statement had my client been, for example, the commander of a concentration camp. Your Honours, I participated in a criminal case in Croatia involving the last living commander of a concentration camp from the Second World War, a case involving several thousands of victims. And it is perfectly clear to me that the Prosecutor could not enumerate all of those several thousand victims who died in the concentration camp, nor could the Court take that into account. However, we have a completely different situation here. My client is held responsible for specific acts, for specific crimes and in respect of specific individuals. And I really have to state, with all due respect to my learned colleague from the Prosecution, that this only testifies to the inability of the Prosecutor to specifically charge for the event. They do not have relevant evidence - they do not have the specific death certificate, for example - except for a very vague story of this witness, which cannot be easily corroborated. It's a hollow story of a witness. And, for example, we are now unable to ask questions relating to his credibility. We are unable to -- I mean, unable. We have been objected to when trying to do so, when we try to challenge the credibility of the witness, because the objection then is that the questions are not relevant. Now, today, we are faced with a murder which was not specifically charged in the indictment, and we have this witness here who is testifying to this murder without any other corroborating evidence. It's not just a single incident -- it's a single incident, and there were not many such cases, there were not many such murders, as many as they could not be specified in the indictment. So I'm really wondering if this is the result of something that actually did not happen but is the result of somebody else's underground and behind-the-scene work. And I'm by no means referring to the Prosecution. I would like to make myself perfectly clear about that. If we have counts 13 to 17 involving Nenad Harmandzic, we could easily have had the same type of counts, the same type of legal qualification involving this particular victim. But this is all we have, and with all due respect I state that they do not have evidence for that. Vinko Martinovic could only be found at the front line, at the Health Centre where he was defending his home and his family. I am perfectly aware, Your Honours, that I should not be making any arguments here, any closing arguments, but I'm really trying to do my best, together with my colleagues, to function in a system which respects fairness. I do not have any doubts as to the fair outcome of the trial; however, I have to draw your attention to the fact that we need to have a fair trial from 9.30 in the morning until 1600 in the afternoon. We should respect the principle of equality of arms and we should also have the right to defence. I really, in all earnestness, appeal to you, Your Honour, to guarantee our right to respond to the charges and to offer our adequate defence. However, we are now faced in the situation where my client is being led into a very unfair position. Charges and allegations are being constantly made throughout these proceedings, new charges, new events. The framework of the events should be explicitly specified in the indictment. We cannot simply allow hollow testimonies with no appropriate corroborating evidence to be heard in this trial. Here we are dealing with an event which is not going to be addressed by anyone else, nor do we have any other piece of evidence to support this allegation, nor was this allegation pled in the indictment, because the legal qualification, as it is, does not cover this particular event. It simply does not correspond to the factual basis of the case, of this particular event, and I beg to disagree with my learned colleague from the Prosecution on this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any response, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Only very briefly, Your Honour, because I'm not going to repeat all the points that have been made in the last several days, and I'm sure the Chamber probably doesn't want me to repeat all that. A couple of things just to clarify, because I was able to check a couple of things during the lunch hour. The statement of this witness was provided to the Martinovic Defence on the 1st of November, 1999, more than two years ago. The statement was then provided to the Naletilic Defence for the first time on the 30th of May, 2000, approximately one and a half years ago. I was then able also to find the original 65 ter summary, which, with the usher's assistance, I would ask to be distributed to the Chamber and to counsel, if it will assist them. On the 11th of October, 2000, Mr. President, Your Honours, more than one year ago, the Prosecutor filed its first list of witnesses pursuant to Rule 65 ter. You'll note by the service sheet, if I can call it that, with the registrar's information on the front page that it was, indeed, filed and distributed to Mr. Seric and Mr. Krsnik. In the excerpt that I have copied here going to paragraphs -- excuse me, pages 55 and 56 concerning this witness's testimony, you will see again there an extensive discussion of what this witness would testify about, including things that he has already touched on, which the Chamber has had an opportunity to hear, the matter in issue now, and other aspects of his testimony, none of which should come as a surprise either to the Defence or, on the Chamber's review of this information, to the Chamber. The basic thrust of this entire witness's evidence, as with virtually all the witnesses, has been laid out for a long time, both for counsel to see and for the Court and its staff to see. So there is no surprise about that, cannot be any unfair surprise about that, we submit. By counsel's logic, Mr. President, they could not know the Prosecution's case or prepare their cross-examination or prepare their case until after the direct examination of each witness was completed, because counsel submits that that is the only time and the first time they know what the Prosecution's case is. Now, Mr. President, respectfully, I submit to you that's not the law and the practice, nor can it be. We cannot have a set of proceedings by which counsel claims that only after the conclusion of the direct examination of each witness, only then can they be prepared to meet the Prosecution's case. We would have to literally stop the trial after every direct examination, if that were the case, until there could be further preparation. In terms of their contesting the facts - and Mr. Seric has quite plainly said they deny that this event ever happened. They contest it - they say there's corroboration. Well, that's a factual dispute, and they will certainly have every opportunity in their case to present their case on this, and the Court will ultimately decide. And at the end of the day, the Chamber may decide that they do not find that the weight of the evidence supports this incident, but that is not a basis not to hear this witness's testimony. They can present their case and make their denials, both through cross-examination, by putting their case to the witness, and in presenting their own case. But I am sure that many things in this case are disputed, and many things in this case, indeed virtually everything, has been denied. But that is not a basis for hearing the Prosecution's evidence. Of course, we have to present our evidence, and then the Chamber will ultimately decide what that evidence shows or does not show. So Mr. President, I've made other -- I've addressed these matters before. We think that there is no question about fair notice. This evidence is clearly relevant to a number of issues in the case, again including such issues as notice, superior authority, and these sorts of things, the acts of their subordinates. And the Chamber should receive them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric, I think we have heard your arguments already, and we heard the response. Do you still want to take the floor? Yes, you may have the floor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Just very briefly, I simply cannot believe that I've heard what I've heard, that we are supposed to prove our innocence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Seric, I don't think that Mr. Scott said that, and I don't think that anybody could possibly interpret what he said as meaning that. What he has said is that he does not accept the principle which you have argued, that you do not know what evidence the Prosecution is going to call until you hear the evidence. The whole point of the Defence receiving a statement and then a summary and then a list of witnesses is to put you on notice not once but three times of the witnesses that they are going to call. There are rules in relation to what evidence can be called. If it is outside the statement, it can't be called because obviously you're surprised. But if it's within the statement, I'd ask you, Mr. Seric, why you didn't avail of the opportunity to either talk to Mr. Scott and his team informally or to use the pre-trial procedures to raise any motions or objections before the Pre-Trial Judge in relation to evidence which, in your view, was inadmissible because it was more prejudicial than probative. Why did you not do that at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I have to say this, Honourable Judge: We did not have the last pre-trial conference which would have given us the opportunity to clear up certain issues either regarding the trial or the timing or any issues like the one you have just raised. Your remark addressed to me is completely appropriate. However, I want to say the following: In the system from which I come from - and I'm in the process of learning here, Honourable Judge - and from what I know, I know that an International Criminal Tribunal is under particular pressure in such cases and the Prosecution is under a lot of pressure, too. Very scrupulous work is required. But what I want to say: I have worked both as a Judge and as a lawyer defending my clients from specific charges, and it is -- it was always stated in this and that period, those charges are alleged, certain crimes were committed. And in my objection to the indictment, which I don't know -- and I don't know how it was supported, and the Pre-Trial Judge Wald also said on several occasions that the indictment is rather too general and imprecise, and that alternative -- and it's full of alternative and cumulative charging. Some charges were even dropped by the Prosecution. But I wanted to see an indictment which would specify specific events transpiring from the supporting material, and if we have got 17 binders full of evidence, and if there is nothing else in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: We are not dealing with the 17 binders. I'm asking you to address to me specifically why, when you're familiar - as it's clear to me from your answer - with pre-trial procedure, and you appeared before a very experienced judge, and you dealt with various objections to the indictment, including dropping some of the charges, why you didn't raise at that stage your objections which you are raising now at the eleventh hour? Why didn't you raise them then? And I'm asking you why didn't you raise them when you received the summaries, and why didn't you raise your objections before this witness came into court, and when you received notice that he was going to be called, why didn't you raise your objections then?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to reiterate, Honourable Judge, today my colleague has examined the witness in such a way that he didn't follow the sequence of the statement. He skipped certain parts. As I have believed all the time until today, that he will not follow through with the specific event, this specific incident, despite the fact that he announced it, I thought that he simply won't do it because there is no other evidence to support this claim. I simply couldn't believe that he will go on with this story, which comes literally out of the blue. I simply couldn't believe that he would decide eventually to put it on the table, and now I believe that everything is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you recall that at the very beginning of this trial, the President encouraged parties on both sides to engage in discussion so you could resolve your differences without taking up court time and issuing motions? Did you attempt to resolve any of your difficulties with Mr. Scott and his assistants before this witness was called?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Honourable Judge Clark, not with regard to this witness. I have already said for what reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I have a question now to address to Mr. Scott. This issue has come up on a number of occasions, where we have heard, or were about to hear, before we were eloquently dissuaded by Mr. Meek not to do so -- where we were about to hear what was described as evidence that was of such a prejudicial nature that for us to hear it at all would cause irreparable damage. Now, on another occasion, we did hear evidence which to me seemed quite startling, but nobody else seemed to share that view, and it passed, and that was in relation to Mr. Andabak and Mr. Naletilic shooting prisoners at point-blank range, and nobody seemed to have any objection to that, so the evidence went in and we will evaluate it at a later stage. But I wanted to know, Mr. Scott, was that under the umbrella of persecution, which you have in your indictment, under which, in your indictment, you have included the word "murder" and "killings" in the early part of the count? Is it -- I've been reading that part, which, in my view - and this is just my personal view - is relevant to what we are talking about today, rather than counts 2 to 8. In my view persecution would be the umbrella crime where, under 34(B) you refer to murdering and wilfully killing Bosnian Muslims. And also I think you referred to it earlier on. Liu knows where it is, but I think it's referred to earlier on in that part of the indictment as well. But is it the custom of the Prosecution not to actually specify a killing which could, if accepted by the Court, amount to murder when you have a direct witness to the killing? Is it the custom to include that in the umbrella of persecution or to actually list it, as Mr. Seric is arguing?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Clark, the answer to your question is: I think I'm not sure I can say there is a custom, to be perfectly candid with the Chamber, given that the practices this institution has evolved and been rather fluid over some years now. I'm not trying to be evasive, but I think that's the honest answer, I submit. It has varied. Obviously, it can be indicated that in some parts of the indictment, such as I turn to, for instance, counts 13 to 17, about Mr. Harmandzic. Obviously, that is quite specific. However, it is our position that there are other parts of the indictment -- and I would agree with you, Judge Clark, and also add that it is covered in the persecutions, but we would respectfully submit that we do believe it's also relevant as to the counts 6, 7, and 8 as well. So I think there are two parts of our argument, and I wouldn't want to completely rely, and don't completely rely, on either one but both, both individually and together. We think there has been fair notice, Judge Clark and Your Honours, Mr. President. I didn't mention -- I failed to mention a while ago because I, indeed, was trying to be quite brief, not to try the Chamber's patience, but I should have noted, as, Judge Clark, you did, there were extensive pre-trial proceedings in this case. Judge Wald presided over a number of hearings a number of status conferences. There were indeed motions challenging the indictment. They were all ruled upon. They were all contested at the time. I have to confess a certain frustration at responding to my learned friend's argument for both accused, because it's always moving. It starts out as a legal issue, and then we are talking about the 17 binders, then we are talking about cumulative charges, then we are talking about alternative charges, and then at the last few minutes, a moment ago, it was the way in which I examined the witness, that I examined a witness in a particular way and apparently it was misleading or deceptive in some way. It's constantly changing. So it's hard to respond to the arguments. I think the indictment is legally sufficient. It has withstood challenges throughout the over a year of pre-trial period. Motions were filed by counsel. They are experienced counsel, admittedly new to this system, as we all are, as we all are. This is a new system for me as well, and I know, Judge Clark, for you and the other. Judges, it's a new system for all of us. But they are experienced and intelligent men and women, and there has been extensive litigation in this case. All these matters could have been resolved a long time ago. I never suggested for one moment that the Defence had to prove their innocence; of course, I would never do that. What the point was is that Mr. Seric seemed to be suggesting that by -- simply by Defence counsel getting up and challenging the evidence of this witness, that somehow we could not have the right to have the evidence. How could we ever proceed? Of course, the Defence has put what might be called a general denial. All we can then do is call our witness, call our evidence, lead the evidence and let the Judges, let you ultimately obviously decide. If the rule was simply every time the Defence disputes something, stands up and says, "We don't accept this witness's testimony," well, then, I guess that's it, it's over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That's not the right way to do it. There have to be rules of procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's our position, Judge Clark. I hope I've answered your question, and if I haven't, I'll try again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: After hearing the views from both parties, especially the answers from both parties to Judge Clark's question, we would like to make two things very clear: This matter involves two aspects. One is the procedural matters, the other is the factual disputes. Here, now, we are not discussing the factual disputes at this moment. We understand the Defence counsel have full right to present their case in the best interests of their clients at that later stage, but now we are only dealing with the procedural matters, that is, whether the disclosure procedure is conducted fairly and timely. After hearing the both parties, we believe that those procedures of disclosure was conducted timely and fairly to the Defence counsel. The previous statement was disclosed to the Defence counsel almost two years ago. And the document of the 95 ter summary was disclosed to Defence counsel almost one year and a half ago. And in that document, page 56, it is clearly listed the incidents we are going to hear about. And there were several opportunities, as Judge Clark put it correctly, that Defence counsel could have raised this but they failed. As a normal practice before this Chamber, if there is no response, we will regard it as an implied agreement. We would not like to see any surprise attack happening in this courtroom. There's another matter I would like to mention, that is, the admission of the evidence and evaluation of the evidence at a later stage. Hearing a witness is a matter; whether we put some weight on the testimony of this witness is another. We believe that it is still too early for us to arrive at any conclusions whether the incidents we are going to hear will fill in the count 6, count 7, and count 8 charged in the indictment, but at least we believe in paragraph 34(B), it is clearly stated that some incidents, including murdering and willful killing, happened at the confrontation line in Mostar, which is fitting the count 1, persecution. Based on this reasoning, we have decided to hear the incidents by that witness. It is so decided. Mr. Scott, you may call your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If the usher can assist, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, before we start, I have a few words of advice for you. You have to understand now you are before an International Tribunal, and before this Tribunal, all persons should be equal, and the accused should be innocent until proved guilty. So no matter whether the -- whether we are sitting or not sitting, any unfriendly gestures to anybody in this courtroom is not allowed. I understand it might be the first time for you to be in the courtroom or in this Tribunal, but I really hope you could understand and bear in mind what I am saying. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Scott. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness QQ, just to bring us back to where we were before the break - and even before that, there had been quite a considerable discussion, so it has been some time since you finished your last testimony - you were talking about a time when you were taken into Mostar and you saw this man named Karso, among other things. And before we proceed, I'm going to ask you if you can assist us, please. Can you be -- give us your best information, as much as you can help us, on the date, the day or the date, when this event occurred and the other events on that day that you are going to tell us about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: I remember very well, but I have one thing to say, if I may. If there is a recording from when we were standing up, I looked at Stela, and he made a gesture with his head, threatening gesture, and I turned to Mr. Scott to draw his attention. I know a lot about Tuta and Stela, and I even haven't begun telling you. I could fill about 200 pages since I know Tuta, Stela, Andabak, Praljak, all of them, and the late Blaz Kraljevic, but I didn't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, we quite understand what happened during the break. Now, we are going to hear your testimony. This Tribunal will make an investigation about what happened during the break. You may answer the question put forward by Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: All right. I'll begin. It was on the 26th of July. Karso got out first off the truck. Several groups were brought from Heliodrom. Fierce fighting went on. There were several occasions like this. Karso was going ahead of me. There was a bridge nearby. I don't know which one. I had never been to Herzegovina before. I have been around a lot, and I know where things happened. And it was when I was digging a ditch for an electrical transmission line or something. There was, together in the cell with me, this guy from Osimitce, Mirsad something, Jakovljevic, I believe, and another man from --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, I think --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're going to have to slow down a bit, again, for the benefit of the interpreters, please, and those of us in the courtroom who do want to very much follow your testimony. So please slow down. While I appreciate the narrative answer, again it will assist us to take things probably in somewhat smaller pieces. Please go ahead -- I want to give you the opportunity to answer the question slowly, please, but don't go too far before we have a chance to take it in pieces, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: All right. I saw one soldier from Zepce. It is wrongly quoted here. It says "70." It's not 70. It's closer to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Really, you have to -- tell him about the little dot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have to watch it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness QQ, there is a number of reasons that make it complicated. Part of them are the protective measures that have been granted for your benefit. For the voice distortion to work -- I should probably have explained this to you sooner, and I apologise. For the voice distortions to work, we cannot be speaking at the same time. I have to turn off my microphone before you can begin to give your answer. If that doesn't happen, there is a chance that your voice will be heard without being distorted. So it is in your own interest, please, that we follow these procedures. Now, if you look toward me please for a moment - if you can look toward me, Witness - you will see on my microphone, there is this red light, and as long as this microphone is on, I'll probably -- I will be asking you a question. I will try to turn it off, as so, and I won't say that I do it perfectly every time, but I will try to turn it off when my question finished. Please do not start answering until you see the red light go off. Also, in addition to being somewhat quick in your speaking, just now you were also dropping off quite to a low level. So not only speak slowly, please, but also keep your voice up. This is only because everyone, including the Chamber, of course, and the Defence, want to hear your testimony. All right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And the translation, and looking at the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could also -- it may also assist you -- I know it's a lot to have in mind, and I know you don't read English, but -- perhaps, perhaps you do some. But if you also look at the translation -- the transcript, excuse me, in front of you on the screen, at least by the words and when they stop and start and the words attributed to me, Mr. Scott, and the words attributed perhaps to others, if you see that stop, that will also give you further indication of what's happening. So I know that's a lot to take in, but assist us, if you can, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, if the witness were to go back to that he'd never been to Herzegovina before, and that there was somebody in the cell with him, from then, I think even the translation has a few spaces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: QQ, let me take you back for a moment. You said that you had not been in Herzegovina before, so let me stop you there. And I don't want you to name your home village or anything such as that. You were from a different part, you grew up and spent most of your life in a different part of Bosnia; is that correct, sir? You can just answer that yes or no. Yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you said you had not been in Herzegovina, at least not very much, before these events in which you were arrested and held during the time that you're telling us about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: No, never. I just passed through Tomislavgrad on one occasion, but I never stopped or spent any significant amount of time before these events, before the war. Before the shooting started; that's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that there was someone in a cell next to you which I think we understood perhaps as someone that provided you information about this, but can you state your answer again about that? What did you mean -- what did you mean to be telling us when you mentioned -- unfortunately, it's gone by on the transcript now, but what did you mean about the person next to you in regard to what you were telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: In the cell in Mostar? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think at this point you were talking, presumably, about the Heliodrom, but I can't really assist you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted] Again, for the reasons that we are trying to protect you and other individuals, I need you not to mention those names. So I'll have to ask those be redacted. And then if you can pause and let me ask -- let me put the question to you again very specifically. I'm not asking you to name -- I'm not asking you to name any prisoner at the moment, but you made reference a few minutes ago to another prisoner who was in a cell next to you about the same time that you said you had not spent much time in Herzegovina before this. Now, did this witness - without naming his name at the moment -- his or her name at the moment - can you explain how it was that this other prisoner assisted you in this regard, if that's what you intended to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Well, we knew each other for a very long time, and several times he gave me some food. There are other reasons as well. Croat, this prisoner, or a Muslim, that's what I cannot remember, if that's what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I may have caused all this confusion and I'm really sorry. He was describing a story how he came -- he was in Mostar, where he hadn't been before, or that he wasn't familiar with. He was digging a ditch for electrical transmission line. There was a bridge nearby. And then we -- it's from -- forget about the other prisoner for the moment, and if we just go back to the -- what happened that day. And I'm sorry if I've confused you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not a problem, of course, Your Honour. I'll try to assist you and the other Judges as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness QQ, let's go back, please, to you're now in Mostar, you've seen this Mr. Karso, you said that you were also -- had been at some point assigned to work in a ditch. Do you remember -- do you remember that? Can we come up to that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes, we can. This Karso person was from Zepce. He did some digging and then left, and then I came to the same spot where he'd been digging. There were several HVO soldiers there. Mr. Stela was there. I'm not saying that it was Stela who did it, but a young man from Zepce who knew Karso, he was a tall man, a good-looking young man, but he had some kind of dispute, quarrel with him. They were quarrelling, and some ugly things were being said and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Sorry, Witness, but again, when you say they were quarrelling, who was quarrelling or who was exchanging words?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: One of the HVO soldiers from Zepce. He was quarrelling with Karso, who is also from Zepce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: He went to see Mr. Stela to ask him something, I don't know what it was all about, because he was further away together with other soldiers, and then I heard Stela, "Well if you really want to do it, go ahead, fuck his balija mother." And then all of a sudden the soldier came back. He pointed his rifle in Karso and he emptied his entire clip into Karso. I felt sick. I closed my eyes. I felt so sorry for the man. Then I was told to pick up a bag and put his body into the bag. Somebody helped me. I don't know who it was. I forgot the name of the person. I don't know where the body ended up. Then there was some confusion, and we were forced to put on uniforms and take some wooden rifles. And Stela at one point in time told me, "You go with the others as well." I have to tell the truth. I hid behind one of the buildings. I didn't want to go because I knew what was -- what would happen. So this confusion lasted for a while, and then it stopped. Some guys had to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apology for interrupting you, but again, before we get away from the Karso incident, let me ask you a few additional questions about that. How far were you, approximately, from where you saw -- you said Stela was there and that you saw this HVO soldier go over and have a conversation with Stela. Approximately how far was Stela from you at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Ten to fifteen metres, thereabouts. I can't remember exactly. Given the trouble we were in, it's hard to remember everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the soldier came back and fired his gun into Karso, how far were you from where Karso was standing at the time he was shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: From where I was?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Two, three, to four metres. Where you are, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was -- as the -- as Karso was being shot and in the immediate seconds and minutes that followed, where was Stela and what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Stela was talking to some soldiers. They were laughing as if nothing had happened, as if only a fly had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, please, did you see Stela do anything to intervene to prevent this from happening, to prevent this soldier from shooting Karso?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness said that Stela was talking up there, which is missing from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Scott, can you clear it up for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll try, Your Honour. I didn't hear that myself, but I'll give the witness a chance to clarify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you can please assist us again, I asked you a few moments ago what Stela was doing at the time that Karso was shot. Can you just answer that question again, please. Where was he, and what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: He was some 20 metres away. He was standing over there with some soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you answered the other question I had put to you, so I won't repeat it. But a different question: After Karso shot this man -- excuse me, my apology. After the soldier shot Karso, did Stela do anything to intervene, say anything to this soldier, or have him arrested or any such thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: No, nothing. At that moment, no. If he did something later on, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you started to go forward with your story. After -- we're finished now with the incident with Mr. Karso. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Somebody brought a black garbage bag. We put his body into this bag. We put it away. I don't know where it ended up. I heard later on that his grave, Karso's grave -- that his grave was found by his family subsequently. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you after you put the body in this bag? We're still on the 26th of July, if I understand you correctly. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Then Stela ordered that we should all go. Some people put on some military uniforms and backpacks full of stones, wooden rifles. Some plastic flasks were put in their pockets, and he forced those people to the line where the BH army was, but I hid behind the building. I'm not ashamed to admit it. They wanted to uncover the positions so that the BH army would shoot them. That was the idea, I guess, so that later on they would be able to see where they were, see where their positions were. But shells were raining down. It was -- there was shooting going on from all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness QQ, I want you to be very clear with the Chamber, please. How far -- how much of this did you actually see? Did there come a point in time when the soldiers dressed in the uniforms and the wooden rifles go out of your sight? I want you to be very clear with the Chamber about what you saw and what you didn't see.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: I knew some of the convicts. I knew some of them. There were five or six soldiers there. And there were detainees in uniforms with wooden rifles but original straps. It really looked like a rifle. They were made by a Muslim carpenter. I know this carpenter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, then, is: As you saw these things happening, did you see these men actually on the confrontation line, or did they set off and at some point go out of your sight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: They left. I could no longer see them. Those buildings were normally inhabited. At one point in time, I lost them out of sight. Later on when I went to Heliodrom, I heard that there were incidents such as killing and wounding. I know that some guys were killed. But anyway, at one point in time, I could no longer see them. Once they reached one of the buildings, they probably moved from one building to another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you go back to the Heliodrom that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did. I was somewhat spared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see all of the men that you saw moving away from you with the uniforms and the rifles? Did you see all of those men come back to the Heliodrom that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: No, because they were scattered around in other rooms. But I heard that some of them were killed. I heard stories from the convicts when the food was distributed, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness QQ, I'm completely changing topics now, just to keep you -- not to confuse you. During the time that you were held at the Heliodrom, did you see any members or components of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of any units that you remember and the approximate time period when you saw these units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Tigers, Pumes, Thunders, 111th Rijeka Unit, the Split Unit. Various brigades were rotating. Tigers had their insignia. Pumes had their own insignia. The Thunders had the sign for electricity. There were two Muslims with the Tigers whom I know. They were quartered at Varda and other locations. When you entered the Heliodrom on the right-hand side, there was the brigade -- the Bruno Busic Brigade in one of those buildings, on that side. There were many of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to seeing the soldiers, the individual members, that is, of these units, did you see vehicles and equipment that these units had with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There were many vehicles, many pinzgauers, trucks which used to belong to the former army but were painted over. There were Howitzers, mortars. There was a sniper unit. There were T-84 tanks. There were 115 millimetre Howitzers. Many various kinds of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the names of the units - and by that I mean Tigrovi, Gromovi, those names - was there anything else identifying these units which indicated to you they were from the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: They were better dressed, better equipped and armed than the HVO. They had the special type of running shoes and tracking shoes, very expensive kind of footwear. I remember their footwear as they were carrying out their dead -- dead Croatian soldiers. I know a lot about that. I haven't told you as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask you a few more questions. Before we ask -- before I ask you that, though, did there come a time when some of these patches and insignias were changed? And if so, will you tell the Chamber about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes, they changed their insignia. They put on the HVO insignia. Some of them had first taken off their old badges, old insignia. Also license plates were taken off, the yellow ones with letters "HV" on it. They put various stickers on their insignia to mark their tanks, stickers that could later on be taken off again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the things that you were required to do as a prisoner, were you ever involved in recovering the bodies of dead soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Once I was required to extinguish some fire. And at one point in time, we had to recover Croatian soldiers. There were more than ten of them. I think that there was a quarrel between the two of them. One could easily recognise them by their footwear. And the Tigers at one point in time left the Heliodrom because of some kind of misunderstanding with the HVO. There were disagreements between the two sides. I don't want to comment on. But they would come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I do want you to clarify. You just said a moment ago -- you said, I think, that there was a quarrel between the two of them. When you say the "two of them," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: The Croatian army and the HVO for Mostar, because the order was to recover bodies of Croatian soldiers first, so they could be transported in helicopter to Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand the disagreement to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Well, this is what I was able to observe. I moved around a lot. I did have some -- I didn't have much restriction of movement, so I was able to observe their quarrels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber approximately -- INTERPRETER: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, please, approximately how many times you were involved in collecting or recovering the bodies of either Croatian or HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: I was there on one occasion near the village of Visnje, which means "cherry tree." There were quite a few cherry trees in the area, and there was a little bridge there I remember. And on another occasion, I was in Malo Polje at the Buna. Many other prisoners did the same job; I mean that of recovering dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sorry, we don't get translation. Yes, can you try again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just would like to draw the attention of this Chamber that -- well, we are following this witness in Croatian, but I have to say that for the past five minutes, many things have not been translated into English. I don't know how to intervene. There are many things that are actually uttered, stated, by the witness, in Croatian or whatever language he is speaking. For example, he said that he didn't like being a witness. Many things are simply not reflected on the record. I don't know. I've discussed it with my colleague. I don't know what to do. On the other hand, I'm receiving the French interpretation all the time. My colleague is not -- cannot hear the witness. We are faced with many technical difficulties here. But what troubles me and worries me most is the fact that many of the things that are stated by the witness are not in the record. A moment ago, he said that he had talked with the secret police in Bosnia, and so on and so forth. Many things are missing from the transcript, sir. I apologise to you, Mr. Witness, but I had to react for the purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm surprised to hear that, because every word the witness said is supposed to be interpreted into the other two languages so that to keep the transcript intact. I'll ask the Registrar to look into this matter at night, I mean to check the recordings and the transcript. And if such things happened in a later stage, you may draw our attention to it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the interpreters would like to state that they are having serious problems with understanding this witness and following the speed with which he is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll try to work with the witness more, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness QQ, I know this is a difficult experience for you, for lots of different reasons, but the interpreters are having a great deal of difficulty accurately translating and reporting your testimony. And I'm sure you can understand that the value of your testimony is greatly limited by -- if it doesn't come through on the record or if it's not understood. So please speak slowly and clearly. I can ask you to be -- if you can be very deliberate, perhaps not in a way that you would be in a conversation with a friend at home, but if you pronounce your words, as I am trying to do, very deliberately and very carefully, it may assist the interpreters. And Mr. Witness, I don't know if what counsel has said is true or not because, unfortunately, I don't speak your language, but please do not make any extraneous comments. Just answer my questions, please, as best you can. All right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: I have to apologise. I always used to speak very fast. My brother would slap me for speaking much too fast. I remember my mother warning me about it. But simply that's the habit I have. I'm trying to concentrate and to speak as slowly as possible. I probably have some gypsy blood in me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. All I can do is ask you, Witness, to think about it deliberately and slow yourself as much as you can, because the judges do want to hear your testimony, as we all do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: I'm trying to do that. Stela made me a little nervous. I tend to get nervous, but I'm trying really hard to speak slowly. I'll try to do my best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You were telling us -- you were in the process of telling us - I think you actually finished - about a number of locations or several locations where you had been involved in collecting bodies. My only final question to you, I think, on that topic is: Were those locations within the boundaries of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS QQ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was in Mostar, near the civilian airport. There was a cherry-tree plantation farm. I remember that I was there on several occasions, so I remember these two locations very well. There are other locations as well, but these are the ones that I remember well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slow, slow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see it's about 4.00, and looking at my outline, I'm about to enter into a topic that I'm sure I can't finish in the next couple of minutes, especially with all the difficulties. This may be as good a place to stop as any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will resume at 9.30 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: 4.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of November, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 24 25
